lessons.title: Egg Incubation Techniques
lessons.body: After your adult flies mate in the cage, females will lay eggs in the small holes of a cardboard egg-carton or a piece of corrugated plastic. You need to collect these eggs every 24 hours. Use a soft paintbrush or a spoon to gently scrape the eggs into a small plastic container. A single female lays about 500 to 900 eggs. A tablespoon of eggs can contain 15,000 to 20,000 eggs. For incubation, you will need a dark, warm place. A plastic bucket with a lid works well. Put a thin layer of moist (not dripping) coco peat or sawdust in the bottom. Place the eggs on top of a small piece of cloth or paper towel. Cover the container with a lid that has small holes for air. Keep the temperature between 27Â°C and 30Â°C. If it is too cold, incubation takes longer; if too hot, eggs dry out. In most African countries, room temperature is fine, but avoid direct sunlight. Humidity should be around 60-70%. You can achieve this by misting the inside of the lid with water every day. Do not spray directly on the eggs. Check the eggs daily. After 3 to 5 days, you will see tiny larvae, about 2-3 mm long, wriggling out. They are ready to be moved to a feeding tray. If you wait too long, they will start to crawl away looking for food. Always wash your hands before handling eggs to avoid contamination. Keep different batches separate to avoid mixing ages.

lessons.title: Handling Neonate Larvae
lessons.body: Neonate larvae are the tiny worms that hatch from the eggs. They are very fragile. You must handle them with care. Do not pick them up with your fingers; you will crush them. Instead, use a soft brush or a small spoon. The best method is to transfer them with the substrate they are on. If you incubated eggs on a piece of cloth, you can place that cloth directly onto the feeding tray. The larvae will crawl off onto the food. If you used a container with coco peat, gently scoop a small amount of the peat with the larvae and spread it on the food. Neonate larvae need to eat within 12 hours of hatching. If they do not find food, they will die. So prepare your feeding tray before the eggs hatch. A good feeding tray is a shallow plastic basin, about 30 cm by 20 cm. Spread a thin layer of feed, about 1 cm thick. The feed should be moist but not wet. You can use ground-up food waste, like fruit peels, vegetable scraps, or brewers' waste. Mash it well so the tiny larvae can eat it. Do not use large chunks. After transferring, cover the tray with a mesh cloth to keep out flies and ants. Keep the tray in a dark place at 28-30Â°C. Check after 24 hours. You should see the larvae actively moving and eating. If many are still on the cloth, leave it for another day. Never expose neonates to direct sunlight or heavy rain. Always keep a clean environment to prevent disease.

lessons.title: Initial Feeding for Neonates
lessons.body: The first meal for neonate larvae is critical. They need soft, moist, and nutrient-rich food. Their mouthparts are very small, so food must be fine. A good starter feed is a mixture of blended fruit waste (mango, papaya, banana) and a little bit of chicken mash or maize bran. You can also use market waste like tomato and cabbage leaves, but blend them into a paste. Avoid citrus fruits like oranges and lemons; they are too acidic and can kill the larvae. Also avoid meat, fish, and oily foods, as they attract pests and cause bad smells. Prepare the feed by grinding it in a blender or by mashing it with a pestle and mortar. Add a little water to make it moist, like a thick paste. Spread this paste on the tray to a depth of about 5 mm. Do not make it too deep, or the larvae will suffocate. For the first 3 days, feed them once a day. A teaspoon of feed per 1000 larvae is enough. After 3 days, they will grow to about 5-7 mm and can eat coarser food. You can then increase the amount and add larger pieces. Always remove any uneaten food after 24 hours to prevent mould and bacteria. If the feed smells bad or turns black, remove it immediately. Keep the tray in a warm, dark place. The larvae should be actively moving and eating. If they are not, check the temperature and moisture. A simple test: if you see them clustering on the food, they are happy. If they crawl away, the feed may be too wet or too dry. Adjust by adding a little bran or water.

lessons.title: Temperature and Humidity Requirements
lessons.body: Black soldier fly larvae grow best at 27Â°C to 30Â°C. If the temperature drops below 20Â°C, they become slow and may stop eating. If it goes above 35Â°C, they can die. In many parts of Africa, daytime temperatures are naturally in this range, but you must protect them from extreme heat. If you are in a hot region, keep the trays in a shaded area or in a room with good ventilation. At night, if it gets cold, you can cover the trays with a blanket or use a small heater, but never place a heater directly next to the trays. Humidity is also important. The ideal relative humidity is 60% to 70%. If the air is too dry, the feed dries out and the larvae cannot eat. If it is too humid, mould grows. To check humidity, you can use a cheap hygrometer, available at most agricultural supply shops. If humidity is low, mist the air around the trays with water, not directly on the larvae. You can also place a shallow pan of water near the trays. If humidity is too high, increase ventilation by opening windows or using a small fan. Do not blow air directly on the trays. For incubation of eggs, keep humidity at 60-70% as well. You can maintain this by placing a wet sponge in the incubation container. Always monitor temperature and humidity daily, ideally twice a day. Keep a simple notebook to record readings. This helps you spot problems early. Remember, sudden changes are more harmful than steady conditions. So avoid moving trays from hot to cold quickly. Consistent warmth and moisture are the keys to healthy neonates.

lessons.title: Preventing Contamination
lessons.body: Contamination is a major cause of failure in BSF farming. It can come from bacteria, mould, ants, or other flies. To prevent it, you must keep everything clean. Always wash your hands with soap before handling eggs, larvae, or feed. Use clean tools: spoons, brushes, and trays should be washed after each use. Do not use the same tools for waste collection and feeding. Keep your incubation and rearing area separate from your waste collection area. If possible, have a dedicated room or shed. Cover all trays with mesh cloth to keep out houseflies, mosquitoes, and ants. The mesh should be fine enough to stop small insects. For ants, you can place the legs of your table in small containers of water, or apply a line of vaseline around the table edge. Never use insecticides near your larvae; they will kill them. If you see mould on the feed, remove it immediately and discard that feed. Mould produces toxins that can kill larvae. Also, remove any dead larvae as soon as you see them. Dead larvae attract more pests and disease. Keep the feed fresh: do not leave feed in the tray for more than 48 hours. If you use food waste, ensure it is not rotten or contaminated with chemicals. Wash fruit and vegetable waste with clean water before feeding. For incubation, sterilise your containers by washing with hot water and soap, then drying in the sun. Do not use bleach or harsh chemicals. If you have multiple batches, keep them separate to avoid cross-contamination. Always start with clean hands, clean tools, and clean environment. A little effort in hygiene saves you from big losses.

lessons.title: Transferring Neonates to Rearing Trays
lessons.body: Once the neonate larvae are 3-4 days old and about 5-7 mm long, they are ready to move to larger rearing trays. Do not wait too long, or they will become overcrowded and stressed. The transfer should be done gently. You can simply lift the small cloth or paper with the larvae and place it on the new tray. If you used a container with substrate, scoop the larvae and substrate together using a soft spoon. Spread them evenly on the new feed. The new tray should be larger, about 60 cm by 40 cm, and have a layer of feed 2-3 cm deep. The feed can be coarser now, like chopped vegetable waste, but still moist. The density should be about 1 gram of larvae per 10 square cm. For example, a tray of 60x40 cm can hold about 240 grams of larvae. If you have more, use multiple trays. After transferring, cover the tray with mesh and keep it in a dark, warm place. Do not feed for the first 6 hours to let them settle. Then add a little feed on top. Check after 24 hours. The larvae should have spread out and be actively feeding. If they cluster in one corner, the tray may be too hot or too cold. Adjust as needed. Keep the tray clean: remove any old feed and dead larvae daily. As they grow, you will need to add more feed and eventually split them into more trays. This transfer is a critical step to ensure healthy growth. Handle them gently, and always maintain hygiene.

quiz.q: How often should you collect BSF eggs from the laying site?
options: D) Only when they turn brown
quiz.explanation: Eggs should be collected daily to prevent them from hatching in the cage and to keep them clean.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for incubating BSF eggs?
quiz.explanation: BSF eggs hatch best at 27-30Â°C; lower temperatures slow development and higher temperatures can kill them.

quiz.q: How long does it take for BSF eggs to hatch under good conditions?
quiz.explanation: At 27-30Â°C, eggs typically hatch in 3 to 5 days.

quiz.q: What tool is best for handling neonate larvae?
quiz.explanation: Neonates are very fragile; a soft brush or spoon prevents crushing them.

quiz.q: How soon after hatching do neonate larvae need to find food?
options: D) They can survive 3 days without food
quiz.explanation: Neonates must eat within 12 hours or they will die of starvation.

quiz.q: What type of feed is best for the first meal of neonate larvae?
options: C) Fine, moist paste of fruit waste
quiz.explanation: Neonates have tiny mouthparts and need soft, moist, finely ground feed.

quiz.q: Which of these should you avoid feeding to neonate larvae?
quiz.explanation: Citrus fruits are too acidic and can kill neonate larvae.

quiz.q: How deep should the feed layer be for neonate larvae?
quiz.explanation: A thin layer of about 5 mm prevents suffocation and allows easy access.

quiz.q: How often should you feed neonate larvae during the first 3 days?
quiz.explanation: Once daily is sufficient for the first 3 days; overfeeding can cause mould.

quiz.q: What is the ideal relative humidity for BSF larvae?
quiz.explanation: 60-70% humidity keeps feed moist and prevents mould growth.

quiz.q: What happens if BSF larvae are kept above 35Â°C?
quiz.explanation: Temperatures above 35Â°C are lethal to BSF larvae.

quiz.q: How can you increase humidity in a BSF rearing room?
options: B) Place a shallow pan of water nearby
quiz.explanation: A pan of water evaporates and raises humidity without wetting the larvae directly.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid sudden temperature changes for neonates?
options: A) It makes them grow faster
B) It causes stress and can kill them
quiz.explanation: Sudden changes stress the larvae and can lead to death; steady conditions are best.

quiz.q: What is a good way to prevent ants from reaching your BSF trays?
options: A) Spray insecticide around the tray
B) Place table legs in containers of water
C) Leave food on the floor
quiz.explanation: Water moats around table legs block ants without harming the larvae.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mould on the feed?
options: A) Mix it into the feed
B) Remove and discard the mouldy feed
quiz.explanation: Mould produces toxins that can kill larvae, so remove it immediately.

quiz.q: How often should you clean your BSF tools and trays?
quiz.explanation: Clean tools after each use to prevent contamination and disease.

quiz.q: Why should you keep incubation and rearing areas separate from waste collection?
options: B) To reduce contamination and pests
quiz.explanation: Separating areas reduces the risk of pests and pathogens from waste entering the clean rearing zone.

quiz.q: When are neonate larvae ready to be transferred to larger rearing trays?
options: B) When they are 3-4 days old and 5-7 mm long
C) When they are 2 weeks old
quiz.explanation: At 3-4 days and 5-7 mm, they are strong enough to handle larger trays and coarser feed.

quiz.q: What is the recommended density for transferring neonate larvae to a rearing tray?
quiz.explanation: A density of about 1 gram of larvae per 10 square cm prevents overcrowding.

quiz.q: How should you transfer neonate larvae from the incubation container?
options: B) Gently scoop with a soft spoon or transfer the cloth
quiz.explanation: Gentle scooping or transferring the cloth avoids injury to the fragile larvae.

quiz.q: What should you do after transferring neonates to a new tray?
options: B) Leave them for 6 hours without feed
quiz.explanation: Letting them settle for 6 hours reduces stress before feeding.

quiz.q: What does it mean if neonate larvae cluster in one corner of the tray?
options: A) They are ready to pupate
B) The tray may be too hot or too cold
quiz.explanation: Clustering often indicates temperature stress; adjust conditions accordingly.

quiz.q: Why is it important to remove dead larvae daily?
options: B) To prevent disease and pests
D) To use them as feed
quiz.explanation: Dead larvae attract pests and can spread disease to healthy larvae.

quiz.q: What is a sign that neonate larvae are happy and feeding well?
options: A) They are crawling away from food
B) They are clustered on the food
quiz.explanation: Clustering on the feed indicates they are actively eating and content.

quiz.q: How can you check humidity in your BSF rearing room?
quiz.explanation: A hygrometer measures relative humidity, available at agricultural supply shops.

quiz.q: What should you do if the feed for neonates is too dry?
options: B) Mist with a little water
quiz.explanation: Misting adds moisture without making the feed too wet.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using insecticides near BSF larvae?
quiz.explanation: Insecticides are toxic to BSF larvae and can wipe out your colony.

quiz.q: What is a good practice before handling eggs or larvae?
quiz.explanation: Washing hands with soap reduces contamination from bacteria and oils.

quiz.q: How often should you monitor temperature and humidity in the rearing room?
quiz.explanation: Twice daily monitoring helps catch and fix issues early.

quiz.q: What is the best way to sterilise incubation containers?
options: B) Wash with hot water and soap, then sun-dry
quiz.explanation: Hot water and soap are effective and safe; sun-drying adds extra sterilisation.
